lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Why Mars Loops Backward
top_level_objectives: Describe apparent retrograde motion as observed from Earth for outer planets
Explain how the heliocentric model accounts for retrograde loops via relative orbital motion, without invoking epicycles
Compare the geocentric epicycle explanation with the heliocentric explanation for retrograde motion
Relate the size of a planet's retrograde loop to its orbital distance and relative speed compared to Earth
Predict how retrograde loop size differs between Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn

scenes.scene_name: Night Sky Puzzle: Mars in Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observational puzzle by letting students watch Mars drift among the stars over simulated weeks and notice the unexpected reversal.
key_visuals: A star field with constellation outlines (e.g., Gemini, Cancer, Leo) as a fixed backdrop
A glowing red marker representing Mars moving along a plotted path night by night
A timestamp/date readout advancing week by week
A faint trailing line showing Mars's path so far
student_actions: Advance time step by step using a control to watch Mars's nightly position
Mark or annotate the point where Mars appears to stop and reverse direction
Record observations of eastward vs westward motion in a short response prompt

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how ancient geocentric astronomers explained retrograde motion using epicycles, setting up the contrast with the heliocentric explanation.
key_visuals: An Earth-centered model with Mars riding on a small circle (epicycle) that itself moves along a larger circle (deferent)
Animated tracing of the resulting looped path projected onto a distant starry sphere
Side-by-side comparison panel showing the epicycle-generated loop next to the observed Mars loop from Scene 1
student_actions: Rotate the epicycle model manually to see how the small circle's motion creates a loop
Toggle between the epicycle model and the observed sky path to compare shapes
Answer a checkpoint question about why this model felt awkward or overly complex

scenes.brief_purpose: Shift the student's viewpoint to a heliocentric vantage point above the solar system plane, introducing the orbits of Earth and Mars.
key_visuals: A top-down view of the Sun with Earth's and Mars's orbital paths drawn as concentric circles
Earth and Mars rendered as small spheres moving along their orbits at different speeds
Speed indicators or arrows showing Earth's faster angular motion compared to Mars
student_actions: Orbit the camera around the solar system model to confirm the circular orbits
Start the simulation and observe Earth completing more orbit distance than Mars in the same time
Note in a short response which planet appears to move faster along its path

scenes.scene_name: The Passing-Car Effect: Building the Loop
scenes.brief_purpose: Let students see how Earth overtaking Mars on the inside track produces the apparent backward loop, using the passing-car analogy as scaffolding.
key_visuals: Split-screen: heliocentric top-down view on one side, Earth-sky view (line of sight to Mars projected onto background stars) on the other
A sight-line ray drawn from Earth to Mars that sweeps forward, pauses, and sweeps backward as Earth passes Mars
An animated highway analogy inset showing a faster car passing a slower car with the slower car's apparent backward drift
student_actions: Run the synchronized animation and watch the sight-line sweep direction change in real time
Pause at the moment Earth passes Mars and identify why the sight-line briefly reverses
Match the passing-car analogy to the orbital motion by labeling which object is 'your car' and which is 'the other car'

scenes.scene_name: Reconstructing the Loop from Both Views
scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate understanding by having students connect the heliocentric motion directly to the originally observed sky loop from Scene 1.
key_visuals: Side-by-side replay: heliocentric orbit animation on the left, resulting star-field loop redrawing on the right in sync
Highlighted correspondence markers showing the same date appearing in both panels simultaneously
The completed retrograde loop shape reappearing, now labeled with the orbital positions that produced each part of the loop
student_actions: Scrub a shared timeline slider and watch both panels update together
Identify the three phases (prograde, retrograde, prograde) on both the orbit view and the sky view
Complete a matching exercise linking orbital positions to points along the sky loop

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the concept by having students compare loop size and duration across the three outer planets to reinforce the distance-speed relationship.
key_visuals: Heliocentric view expanded to include Jupiter's and Saturn's orbits alongside Mars's
Three separate small inset sky-view panels each showing the retrograde loop shape for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn at the same scale
A data table overlay showing orbital period, distance from Sun, and loop angular size for each planet
student_actions: Run the simulation for all three planets and visually compare loop sizes
Rank the planets from largest to smallest apparent loop and justify the ranking using orbital speed and distance
Answer a reflection question predicting how a hypothetical planet even farther than Saturn would behave

scenes.scene_name: Synthesis: From Geocentric Puzzle to Heliocentric Clarity
scenes.brief_purpose: Wrap up the lab by having students articulate why the heliocentric model is the simpler, more natural explanation for retrograde motion.
key_visuals: A final split view: the cluttered epicycle diagram from Scene 2 next to the clean heliocentric orbit diagram
A summary timeline of the historical shift from geocentric to heliocentric models with key figures (Ptolemy, Copernicus, Kepler) labeled
A recap animation of Mars's loop forming naturally from relative orbital motion
student_actions: Write a short comparison explaining why the heliocentric model requires no epicycles to explain the loop
Complete a concluding quiz question connecting relative speed, orbital distance, and apparent retrograde motion
Reflect on how this observation historically served as evidence favoring heliocentrism
